In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. [May Allah send blessings upon Muhammad and his family, and grant them abundant peace. [[Note in the margin: Ya.]]]

[Tafsir of Surah Ibrahim, all of it Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah and Jabir. Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: except for two of its verses, which are Medinan. It was also said: three verses, revealed concerning those who waged war against Allah and His Messenger, namely His Exalted saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for ingratitude﴾ [Ibrahim: 28] up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, your destination is the Fire﴾ [Ibrahim: 30].]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. [This is] a Book We have sent down to you, [O Muhammad], that you may bring mankind from darknesses into light, by the permission of their Lord, to the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy﴾ (1)

His Exalted saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book We have sent down to you﴾ — its meaning has already been discussed.

(That you may bring mankind) i.e., by means of the Book, which is the Qur'an, i.e., by your calling them to it.

(From darknesses into light) i.e., from the darknesses of disbelief, misguidance and ignorance into the light of faith and knowledge. This is figurative, since disbelief is like darkness and Islam is like light. It was also said: from innovation to the Sunnah, and from doubt to certainty; the meanings are close.

(By the permission of their Lord) i.e., by His granting them success and His kindness toward them. The preposition "bi" in "bi-idhni Rabbihim" is connected to "li-tukhrija." The act is attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ) because he is the caller, the warner and the guide.

(To the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy) It is like your saying: "I went out to Zayd the intelligent, the virtuous," without a conjunction, because they are one thing. Allah is the Exalted in Might, who has no like and no semblance. It was also said: "al-'Aziz" is the One whom no conqueror can overcome. It was also said: "al-'Aziz" is the Invincible in His dominion and authority. "Al-Hamid" means the One praised by every tongue, and glorified in every place in every state. Miqsam narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Some people believed in 'Isa ibn Maryam and others disbelieved in him. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, those who had disbelieved in 'Isa believed in him, and those who had believed in 'Isa disbelieved. So this verse was revealed. Al-Mawardi mentioned it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 2–3:

Allah's saying: ﴿Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning: (He is) the Owner, the Master, the Originator and the Creator. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, and others, read "Allahu" with a nominative (raf') vowel, as the subject (mubtada'), with "alladhi" as its predicate (khabar). It has also been said that "alladhi" is a qualifier (sifah), and the predicate is implied, meaning: Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, is capable of all things. The rest read it with a genitive (khafd) vowel, as an epithet (na't) for "al-'Aziz al-Hamid", thus placing the epithet before the thing described, as in your saying: "I passed by the handsome Zayd" (marartu bi-al-zarif Zayd). It has also been said that it is in apposition (badal) to "al-Hamid" and not a qualifier, because the name Allah has become like a proper name ( 'alam), and so it is not described, just as one does not describe (someone) as Zayd or 'Amr. Rather, it may be described by it in meaning, since its meaning is that He alone is the One who has the power of bringing into existence. Abu 'Amr said: the genitive is by way of transposition (taqdim wa-ta'khir); its implied sense is: "To the path of Allah, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, He to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth." Ya'qub, when he paused on "al-Hamid", would read it with a nominative vowel, and when he continued would read it with a genitive vowel as an epithet. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever reads with the genitive makes a pause at "wa-ma fi al-ard".

Allah's saying: ﴿And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment﴾. The meaning of "woe" (al-waylu) has already been mentioned in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 7 onward.]]. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a word said for punishment and destruction. "From a severe punishment", meaning: from Hell.

(Those who prefer the worldly life) meaning: they choose it over the Hereafter, and the disbelievers do this. So "alladhina" is in the genitive position as a qualifier of them. It has also been said that it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: they are those who... It has also been said that "alladhina yastahibbuna" is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is "ulaika". Anyone who prefers the world and its splendour, and loves to remain in its bounties over the bounties of the Hereafter, and turns people away from the path of Allah—that is, turns people away from it, which is the religion of Allah that the Messengers brought, according to the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and others—is included in this verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What I fear most for my community are the misleading leaders (al-a'immah al-mudilluna)," and it is a sound hadith. How numerous they are in these times, and Allah is the One sought for help. It has also been said: "yastahibbuna" means they seek the world by unlawful means, because the blessing of Allah is only sought through obedience to Him, not through disobedience.

(And they seek to make it crooked) meaning: they seek for it deviation and inclination, to match their desires and to fulfil their needs and aims. "Al-sabil" may be masculine or feminine. "Al-'iwaj" with a kasrah on the 'ayn is used for religion, matters, and the earth, and for everything that is not upright; and with a fathah on the 'ayn for everything that is upright, such as a wall, a spear, and the like. This has been mentioned in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 154.]] and elsewhere.

(Those are in far-off error) meaning: a departure from the truth, far from it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*) on surah 14, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send any messenger﴾, meaning before you, O Muhammad, (ﷺ), (**except in the language of his people**), meaning in their tongue, so that he might make clear to them the matter of their religion. He used the singular "tongue" (*lisan*), although it is attributed to "the people," because what is meant is the language (*lughah*). It is a generic noun (*ism jins*), which applies to the few and the many. There is no proof in this verse for the non-Arabs (*al-'ajam*) and others, because whoever is given a translation of what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, in a form he can understand, is bound by the proof. Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good news and a warner to all mankind﴾ [Saba': 28]. [[See vol. 14, p. 300.]]

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "Every prophet was sent to his own people in their tongue, and Allah sent me to every red and black person of His creation." He (ﷺ) further said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, no one from this nation hears of me, whether Jew or Christian, and then does not believe in what I have been sent with, except that he will be among the companions of the Fire." Muslim recorded it, and it has passed before.

His saying: ﴿So Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾. This is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (the sect that denies the all-encompassing divine will and decree) regarding the executing of the will. It is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*), and it is not conjoined to "that he might make clear," because the sending occurred for the sake of clarification, not for the sake of misguidance. It is permissible to put "yudill" in the subjunctive (*nasb*), because the sending became a cause of misguidance, so it is like His saying: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. [[See vol. 13, p. 252.]] The sending became a cause of misguidance because they disbelieved in it when it came to them, so it became as though it were the cause of their disbelief.

﴿He is the Mighty﴾: its meaning has already been mentioned.

"And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs" (wa-laqad arsalna Musa bi-ayatina): that is, with Our proofs and Our evidences, meaning the miracles that indicate the truth of his prophethood. Mujahid said: they are the nine signs [[The nine signs are: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the staff and his hand, the years of drought, and the shortage of fruits.]].

("Bring out your people from the darknesses into the light"): its parallel is the Exalted's saying, addressed to our Prophet ﷺ at the beginning of the surah: "That you may bring out mankind from the darknesses into the light" (li-tukhrija al-nas min al-zulumat ila al-nur). Here "an" (that) is in the sense of "i" (namely), as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿And the eminent ones among them went forth, saying: Walk on﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 151.]] [p. 6] i.e., "Walk on."

The Exalted's saying: "And remind them of the Days of Allah" (wa-dhakkirhum bi-ayyam Allah): that is, speak to them in words by which they will remember the Days of Allah the Exalted. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: "with the blessings of Allah upon them." Ubayy ibn Ka'b also said this, and narrated it as a marfu' report: that is, with what Allah bestowed upon them of deliverance from Pharaoh and from the wandering in the wilderness, and all other blessings. The blessings are sometimes called "days," and from this is the verse of Amr ibn Kulthum [[The line is from his Mu'allaqa, and its full form is:

"We disobeyed the king in them, that we should submit"

It may also be that calling them "bright" (ghurr) is because of their elevation above the king and their refusal of him, so their days are bright for them and long against their enemies; accordingly there is no proof in the line that "days" means "blessings." "Ayyam" in the genitive is conjoined to "bi-anna" in the line before it, and it is permissible to take the waw as a substitute for "rubba."]]:

"And days for us, bright and long."

Also from Ibn Abbas and Muqatil: with the events of Allah among the earlier nations. It is said: "So-and-so is knowledgeable about the days of the Arabs," meaning about their battles. Ibn Zayd said: it means the days in which He took vengeance upon the bygone nations. Likewise Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik, who said: "His trials." Al-Tabari said: admonish them with what passed for them in the past days, that is, with what occurred in the days of Allah of blessing and trial, when they were enslaved and humiliated. He dispensed with mentioning the blessing because the days were known to them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "While Musa, peace be upon him, was among his people reminding them of the Days of Allah, and the Days of Allah are His trials and His bounties," and he mentioned the hadith of al-Khidr. This indicates the permissibility of admonition that softens the hearts and strengthens certainty, free of every innovation and cleansed of every misguidance and doubt.

("Indeed in that") that is, in reminding them of the Days of Allah ("are signs"): that is, indications.

("For every steadfast one") that is, one who is very patient in obeying Allah and in refraining from His disobedience.

("Grateful"): for the blessings of Allah. Qatadah said: he is the servant who, when given, gives thanks, and when tried, is patient. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Faith is of two halves: half patience and half gratitude," then he recited this verse: "Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one." Similar is narrated from al-Sha'bi as a mawquf report. Al-Hasan al-Basri hid from al-Hajjaj for seven years, and when news of his death reached him he said: "O Allah, You have caused him to die, so cause his sunnah to die," and he prostrated in thanks and recited: "Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one." The signs are specifically assigned to every steadfast, grateful one because he takes heed from them and does not neglect them, as He said: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 207.]] [al-Nazi'at: 45], though he is a warner to all.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 6–7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when Moses said to his people, "Remember the favor of Allah upon you when He saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who were afflicting you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive; and in that was a great trial from your Lord."﴾ This has already been discussed fully in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 331.]], and all praise is due to Allah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed﴾. It has been said: this is from the speech of Moses to his people. And it has been said: it is from the speech of Allah, meaning: "And remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord said such-and-such." "Ta'adhdhana" and "adhdhana" have the same meaning, "to inform," like "awda'a" and "tawa'ada" (to threaten). This meaning has been narrated from al-Hasan and others. From it comes the "adhan" (call to prayer), because it is an announcement. The poet said:

*We did not perceive the light of dawn until / we heard the announcer (al-adhin) in our gatherings.*

Ibn Mas'ud used to recite: "And when your Lord said," and the meaning is the same.

﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾, meaning: if you are grateful for My bounty, I will surely increase you from My grace. Al-Hasan said: if you are grateful for My favor, I will increase you in obedience to Me. Ibn 'Abbas said: if you affirm the Oneness [of Allah] and obey [Him], I will increase you in reward. The meanings of these statements are close, and the verse explicitly states that gratitude is the cause of increase. The views of the scholars on the meaning of gratitude have already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 171 ff.]]. One of the righteous was asked about gratitude to Allah and said: "That you strengthen yourself with His blessings against His disobedience." It is related from Dawud, peace be upon him, that he said: "My Lord, how can I thank You, when my thanking You is itself a renewed blessing from You upon me?" He said: "O Dawud, now you have thanked Me." I say: the reality of gratitude, according to this, is acknowledging the blessing as coming from its Giver, and not spending it in other than His obedience. Al-Hadi recited while he was eating:

*He granted you His provision so that you would stand in it / in His obedience, and thank Him for some of His due right.*

*You did not thank Him for His blessing, but rather / you grew strong in disobeying Him through His provision.*

Then he choked on the morsel, and the tear strangled him. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: when you hear the mention of gratitude, prepare yourself for increase.

﴿But if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe﴾, meaning: you deny My right. It has been said: [you deny] My blessings. He promised punishment for disbelief just as He promised increase for gratitude. The fa' that would be in the response of the conditional after "inna" has been omitted, due to its being well known.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 8–9:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on earth all together, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾. That is, no deficiency reaches Him by that; rather He is the Self-sufficient (al-Ghani). "Al-Hamid" means the One who is praised (al-Mahmud).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Has there not come to you the news (naba') of those before you, the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud﴾. Al-naba' is the report, and its plural is al-anba'. The poet said:

"Has there not come to you, and the reports spread..."

[Note: the speaker is Qays ibn Zuhayr; the full line is: "by what the she-camels of the sons of Ziyad encountered", and after it: "and their retention with the Qurashi was bought with coats of mail and sharp swords." The sons of Ziyad: al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad and his brothers. Qays took a coat of mail from al-Rabi', so Qays drove al-Rabi's camels to Mecca and sold them to ʿAbd Allah ibn Jadʿan — and by "the Qurashi" he means him — for coats of mail and swords.]

Then it was said: it is from the words of Moses. And it was said: it is from the words of Allah, meaning: "And remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord said such-and-such." And it was said: it is the beginning of an address from Allah the Exalted. The account of the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud is well known, which Allah related in His Book. As for His words: ﴿and those after them, none knows them but Allah﴾, that is, none counts their number but Allah, and none knows their lineage but Allah. The genealogists (al-nassabun), even though they trace lineages back to Adam, do not claim to have enumerated all the nations; they only trace some, and refrain from tracing others. It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he heard genealogists tracing lineage to Maʿd ibn ʿAdnan and then adding to it, he said: "The genealogists have lied; Allah says: 'None knows them but Allah.'" It has also been related from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "We have found no one who knows what lies between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil there are thirty fathers who are not known." Ibn Masʿud, when he recited, would say: "None knows them but Allah," and then say: "The genealogists have lied."

﴿Their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾, that is, with the arguments and evidences.

﴿So they put their hands into their mouths﴾. That is, those people put their own hands into their mouths to bite them in rage [from Ibn ʿAbbas's narration; in some copies: "to bite"] at what the messengers brought, since it contained the foolishness of their intellects and the reviling of their idols. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said likewise, reciting: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ [Al ʿImran: 119]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when they heard the Book of Allah they marvelled and returned their hands to their mouths. Abu Salih said: when their prophet said to them, "I am the messenger of Allah to you," they pointed with their fingers to their mouths, meaning: "Be silent," denying him and rejecting his words. These three opinions are close in meaning. The two pronouns refer to the disbelievers, and the first opinion is the soundest in its chain. Abu ʿUbayd said: Ibn Mahdi related to us from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from ʿAbd Allah concerning His words "so they put their hands into their mouths": he said, "They bit them in rage." The poet said:

"If only Salma had seen my wasting [the flesh shaking from emaciation] and the slenderness in the bone of my shin and my hand,
and the distance of my family and the harshness of my kin,
she would have bitten the tips of her hand from passion."

This meaning has already been explained in Al ʿImran, and praise is to Allah. Mujahid and Qatadah said: they returned their words to the messengers and denied them with their mouths, so the first pronoun is for the messengers and the second for the disbelievers. Al-Hasan and others said: they placed their hands in the mouths of the messengers as a rejection of what they said, so on this view the first pronoun is for the disbelievers and the second for the messengers. It was also said: it means they gestured to the messengers to be silent. Muqatil said: they took the hands of the messengers and placed them over the messengers' mouths to silence them and cut off their speech. It was also said: the messengers returned the hands of the people into their mouths. It was also said: the "hands" here means blessings, i.e., they rejected the blessings of the messengers with their mouths, that is, with speech and denial; and the coming of the messengers with the laws is a blessing. The meaning is: they denied with their mouths what the messengers brought. The "fi" here means "bi," as one says: "I sat in the house" and "I sat at the house." Particles of attribute may stand in place of one another. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is a figure of speech, meaning they did not believe and did not respond; the Arabs say of a man who withholds an answer and falls silent: "He has put his hand into his mouth." Al-Akhfash also said this. Al-Qutabi said: we have not heard any Arab say "he returned his hand into his mouth" when he abandons what he was commanded. Al-Mughni said: they bit their hands out of rage and fury, citing the poet's line:

"You pour into his mouth the poison of envy until he bites his palms,"

meaning that they enrage the envious until he bites his fingers and palms. Another said:

"He has consumed his fingertips by biting, so he now bites his hoof [the part from the wrist to the joint of the shin]."

And they said (meaning the nations to the messengers): ﴿Indeed we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾, that is, in your being sent, according to your claim; not that they acknowledged that they had been sent.

﴿And indeed we are in doubt﴾, that is, in suspicion and uncertainty,

﴿about that to which you call us﴾, namely monotheism,

﴿disquieting﴾, that is, causing unease; one says "arabtuhu" when one does something that brings about doubt and uncertainty. That is, we suppose that you seek kingship and worldly gain.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 8–9:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on earth all together, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾. That is, no deficiency reaches Him by that; rather He is the Self-sufficient (al-Ghani). "Al-Hamid" means the One who is praised (al-Mahmud).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Has there not come to you the news (naba') of those before you, the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud﴾. Al-naba' is the report, and its plural is al-anba'. The poet said:

"Has there not come to you, and the reports spread..."

[Note: the speaker is Qays ibn Zuhayr; the full line is: "by what the she-camels of the sons of Ziyad encountered", and after it: "and their retention with the Qurashi was bought with coats of mail and sharp swords." The sons of Ziyad: al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad and his brothers. Qays took a coat of mail from al-Rabi', so Qays drove al-Rabi's camels to Mecca and sold them to ʿAbd Allah ibn Jadʿan — and by "the Qurashi" he means him — for coats of mail and swords.]

Then it was said: it is from the words of Moses. And it was said: it is from the words of Allah, meaning: "And remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord said such-and-such." And it was said: it is the beginning of an address from Allah the Exalted. The account of the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud is well known, which Allah related in His Book. As for His words: ﴿and those after them, none knows them but Allah﴾, that is, none counts their number but Allah, and none knows their lineage but Allah. The genealogists (al-nassabun), even though they trace lineages back to Adam, do not claim to have enumerated all the nations; they only trace some, and refrain from tracing others. It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he heard genealogists tracing lineage to Maʿd ibn ʿAdnan and then adding to it, he said: "The genealogists have lied; Allah says: 'None knows them but Allah.'" It has also been related from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "We have found no one who knows what lies between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil there are thirty fathers who are not known." Ibn Masʿud, when he recited, would say: "None knows them but Allah," and then say: "The genealogists have lied."

﴿Their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾, that is, with the arguments and evidences.

﴿So they put their hands into their mouths﴾. That is, those people put their own hands into their mouths to bite them in rage [from Ibn ʿAbbas's narration; in some copies: "to bite"] at what the messengers brought, since it contained the foolishness of their intellects and the reviling of their idols. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said likewise, reciting: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ [Al ʿImran: 119]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when they heard the Book of Allah they marvelled and returned their hands to their mouths. Abu Salih said: when their prophet said to them, "I am the messenger of Allah to you," they pointed with their fingers to their mouths, meaning: "Be silent," denying him and rejecting his words. These three opinions are close in meaning. The two pronouns refer to the disbelievers, and the first opinion is the soundest in its chain. Abu ʿUbayd said: Ibn Mahdi related to us from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from ʿAbd Allah concerning His words "so they put their hands into their mouths": he said, "They bit them in rage." The poet said:

"If only Salma had seen my wasting [the flesh shaking from emaciation] and the slenderness in the bone of my shin and my hand,
and the distance of my family and the harshness of my kin,
she would have bitten the tips of her hand from passion."

This meaning has already been explained in Al ʿImran, and praise is to Allah. Mujahid and Qatadah said: they returned their words to the messengers and denied them with their mouths, so the first pronoun is for the messengers and the second for the disbelievers. Al-Hasan and others said: they placed their hands in the mouths of the messengers as a rejection of what they said, so on this view the first pronoun is for the disbelievers and the second for the messengers. It was also said: it means they gestured to the messengers to be silent. Muqatil said: they took the hands of the messengers and placed them over the messengers' mouths to silence them and cut off their speech. It was also said: the messengers returned the hands of the people into their mouths. It was also said: the "hands" here means blessings, i.e., they rejected the blessings of the messengers with their mouths, that is, with speech and denial; and the coming of the messengers with the laws is a blessing. The meaning is: they denied with their mouths what the messengers brought. The "fi" here means "bi," as one says: "I sat in the house" and "I sat at the house." Particles of attribute may stand in place of one another. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is a figure of speech, meaning they did not believe and did not respond; the Arabs say of a man who withholds an answer and falls silent: "He has put his hand into his mouth." Al-Akhfash also said this. Al-Qutabi said: we have not heard any Arab say "he returned his hand into his mouth" when he abandons what he was commanded. Al-Mughni said: they bit their hands out of rage and fury, citing the poet's line:

"You pour into his mouth the poison of envy until he bites his palms,"

meaning that they enrage the envious until he bites his fingers and palms. Another said:

"He has consumed his fingertips by biting, so he now bites his hoof [the part from the wrist to the joint of the shin]."

And they said (meaning the nations to the messengers): ﴿Indeed we disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾, that is, in your being sent, according to your claim; not that they acknowledged that they had been sent.

﴿And indeed we are in doubt﴾, that is, in suspicion and uncertainty,

﴿about that to which you call us﴾, namely monotheism,

﴿disquieting﴾, that is, causing unease; one says "arabtuhu" when one does something that brings about doubt and uncertainty. That is, we suppose that you seek kingship and worldly gain.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Their messengers said to them﴾ is a question whose meaning is denial, i.e., there is no doubt about Allah, that is, about His oneness (tawhid), said Qatadah. It was also said: about His obedience (ta'ah). And it may carry a third meaning: Is there doubt about the power of Allah? Because they agree upon it and disagree about everything else. His saying confirms this: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, its Creator, its Innovator, its Producer, and its Bringer into existence after non-existence, to draw attention to His power, so that worship is not permissible except to Him.

﴿He calls you﴾, i.e., to His obedience through the messengers and the books.

﴿That He may forgive you of your sins﴾. Abu Ubayd said: "min" (of) is extra (ziyadah, redundant). Sibawayh said: it is for partitive (tab'id), and it is permissible to mention the part while meaning the whole.

It was also said: "min" is for substitution (badal) and is neither extra nor partitive, i.e., so that forgiveness will be a substitute for the sins.

﴿And defer you to a specified term﴾, meaning death, so that He does not punish you in this world.

﴿They said: You are not⁠﴾, i.e., what you are not.

﴿but mortals like us﴾ in appearance and form, eating what we eat and drinking what we drink, and you are not angels.

﴿You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship﴾ of idols and images, ﴿so bring us a clear authority﴾, i.e., a manifest proof. This was impossible for them, for the messengers only called people while accompanied by miracles.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 11–12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their messengers said to them: "We are only humans like you"﴾, meaning in form and appearance, as you have said.

(But God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants), meaning He graces him with prophethood. It is also said: with success (tawfiq), wisdom, knowledge and guidance. Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: with the recitation of the Qur'an and understanding of what is in it. I say: this is a good opinion, and al-Tabari has transmitted from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, who said: "I said to Abu Dharr: 'O uncle, advise me.' He said: 'I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as you have asked me, and he said: "There is no day, nor night, nor hour, except that God has in it a charity (sadaqah) by which He bestows favour upon whomever He wills of His servants. And God, exalted is He, has not bestowed favour upon His servants with anything like inspiring them to remember Him."'"

(And it is not for us to bring you any authority), meaning any proof or sign.

(Except by the permission of God), meaning by His will; and that is not within our power. That is, we cannot bring a proof as you demand except by His command and power. Its wording is that of a statement, but its meaning is negation, because one does not prohibit anyone from what they are not able to do.

(And upon God let the believers rely), its meaning has already been mentioned.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And why should we not rely upon God?﴾ "Ma" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), "lana" is the predicate (khabar), and what follows it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The implied sense: what reason do we have for not relying upon God?

(And He has guided us to our paths), meaning the way that leads to His mercy and saves from His wrath and vengeance.

(And we will surely be patient) — the lam is the lam of oath; its implied sense is: "By God, we will surely be patient" (over what you have inflicted upon us), meaning of insult and beating, denial and killing, trusting in God that He will suffice us and reward us.

(And upon God let those who rely [upon Him] rely).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 13–14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to their messengers, "We will surely expel you from our land"﴾. The lam is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), meaning: "By Allah, we will surely expel you."

(Or you must return to our creed) meaning: until you return, or unless you return; this was said by al-Tabari and others. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This does not need this interpretation, for 'aw' retains its usual meaning of choice (al-takhyir). The disbelievers gave the messengers a choice between returning to their religion or being expelled from their land. This is the way of Allah, exalted is He, with His messengers and His servants. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And indeed, they almost drove you from the land to expel you from it, but then they would not remain after you except for a little. [It was] the practice concerning those We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [al-Isra: 76–77]?" And this meaning has already been discussed in (Surah) al-A'raf and elsewhere.

(In our religion) meaning: to our religion. (Then their Lord revealed to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers. And We will surely settle you in the land after them.")

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is for those who fear My standing [before Me] and fear My warning﴾. Meaning: His standing before Me on the Day of Resurrection, so the verbal noun is attributed to its agent. The maqam is a verbal noun like al-qiyam; it is said: qama qiyaman and maqaman. He attributed it to Himself because it is specific to Him. The maqam with a fatha on the mim means a place of standing, and with a damma it means the act of establishing. "That is for those who fear My maqam" means My standing over him and My watching over him. Allah, exalted is He, said: "Is then He who is standing over every soul in what it has earned [like those who associate partners with Him]?" [al-Ra'd: 33]. Al-Akhfash said: "That is for those who fear My maqam" means My punishment, "and fear My warning" means the Qur'an and its admonitions. It was also said that it is the punishment. And al-wa'id is the noun from al-wa'd.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 14, verses 15–17:**

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And they sought victory﴾, means they sought help (istinsar). That is, He permitted the messengers to seek victory over their peoples and to pray for their destruction. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and others. It has already been discussed in *al-Baqarah* [See vol. 2, p. 26 ff.]. From this is the hadith (a reported saying of the Prophet) that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to seek victory through the destitute emigrants (sa'alik al-muhajirin), meaning he sought help through them. Ibn Zayd said: the nations sought victory by supplication, as the Quraysh said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and so on. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said that the Messenger said: "My people have denied me, so decide between me and them a decisive decision." And the nations said: "If these are truthful, then punish us." This too is from Ibn 'Abbas. A parallel to it is: ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah if you are among the truthful﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29], and ﴿Bring us what you promise us if you are among the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 77].

(And every obstinate tyrant was disappointed.) The jabbar is the arrogant one who sees no right of anyone over him; this is how the lexicographers define it, as mentioned by al-Nahhas. The 'anid is one who opposes the truth and turns away from it, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is said: 'anada 'an qawmihi, meaning he distanced himself from his people. It was also said that it derives from al-'anad, which means a side, and 'a'anda fulan means he took a side turning away. The poet said:

*When I descend, make me a middle [in the ranks],*
*For I am old and cannot bear the 'unnad.*

Al-Harawi said: the words ﴿jabbar 'anid﴾ mean one who deviates from the right course; he is al-'anud, al-'anid, and al-'annid. In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas concerning the menstruating-like bleeding (istihadah), when he was asked about it, he said: "It is a 'irq 'annid" (a persistent vein). Abu 'Ubayd said: it is the one that deviates and transgresses, like a person who is obstinate; this vein, because of the abundance of what flows from it, has this status. Shamir said: the 'annid is that which does not stop. 'Umar, describing his own conduct, said: "I hold back the 'anud." Al-Layth said: the 'anud among camels is the one that never mixes with the herd but always remains on the side. He meant: whoever intends to oppose or to separate from the community, I turn him back to it. Muqatil said: the 'anid is the arrogant one. Ibn Kaysan said: he is the one who holds his nose high. It was also said: the 'anud and 'anid are those who are arrogant toward the messengers and go astray from the path of truth, so they do not follow it. The Arabs say: the worst of camels is the 'anud, the one that strays from the road. It was also said: the 'anid is the disobedient. Qatada said: the 'anid is the one who refuses to say: "There is no god but Allah."

I say: the jabbar and the 'anid in the verse have one meaning, even though the wording differs. Everyone who is far from the truth is a jabbar and an 'anid, that is, arrogant. It was also said that what is meant in the verse is Abu Jahl; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

Al-Mawardi, in his book *Adab al-Dunya wa al-Din*, related that al-Walid ibn Yazid ibn 'Abd al-Malik once sought an omen (tafa'ul) in the Mushaf, and there came up for him the words of the Mighty and Majestic: "And they sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed." He tore up the Mushaf and began to recite:

*Do you threaten every obstinate tyrant?*
*Here I am, that tyrant, that obstinate one.*

*When you come before your Lord on the Day of Gathering,*
*Say: "O Lord, al-Walid tore me apart."*

He did not remain [except] for a few days before he was killed in the worst manner, and his head was hung upon his palace, and then upon the wall of his city.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Behind him is Hell﴾, means: behind that disbeliever is Hell, that is, after his destruction. The word *wara'* means *ba'd* (after). The poet al-Nabigha said:

*I swore, and I left no doubt for you [in your heart],*
*And there is no refuge for a man beyond Allah.*

That is, after Allah, may His majesty be exalted. Likewise His statement: ﴿And behind him is a severe punishment﴾, meaning after him. And His statement: ﴿and they disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], meaning what is other than it; this was said by al-Farra'. Abu 'Ubayd said: "after it." It was also said: "behind him" means in front of him, and from this is the poet's statement:

*And behind you is a day you will reach,*
*Neither one present who can escape it, nor one who is hidden from it.*

Another said:

*Do the Banu Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience,*
*While my people Tamim and the deserts are behind me?*

And Labid said:

*Is it not behind me, if my death comes upon me,*
*Only the staff, around which the fingers bend?*

He means: in front of me. In the revelation: ﴿There was behind them a king﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning in front of them. To this view went Abu 'Ubayda, Abu 'Ali Qutrub, and others. Al-Akhfash said: it is like saying, "This matter is behind you," meaning it will come to you; and "I am behind it," meaning I am in pursuit of it and will reach it. Al-Nahhas said regarding ﴿Behind him is Hell﴾ that it means in front of him; it is not one of the words with opposite meanings (addad), but derives from *tawara*, meaning to be hidden. Al-Azhari said: *wara'* can mean both behind and in front, so it is one of the addad; Abu 'Ubayda also said this. Their derivation is from what is hidden and concealed, for Hell is concealed and not seen, so it is called "behind" because it is not seen. Ibn al-Anbari related this, and it is a good explanation.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And he will be given to drink of water like pus﴾, means water like pus, just as one says of a brave man, "He is a lion," meaning like a lion; this is a figure of speech and comparison. It was also said that it is what flows from the bodies of the people of the Fire of pus and blood. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is the washing water of the people of the Fire, which flows from the private parts of fornicators (adulterers and adulteresses). It was also said: it is water that he finds repulsive and turns away from, so the word *sadid* (pus) is derived from *sadd* (turning away). Ibn al-Mubarak related: Safwan ibn 'Amr informed us, on the authority of Ubayd Allah ibn Busr, on the authority of Abu Umama, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His statement: ﴿And he will be given to drink of water like pus, which he will gulp down﴾. He said: it is brought near to his mouth, and he dislikes it; when it is brought closer to him, it scorches his face and the skin of his head falls off; and when he drinks it, it cuts his intestines until they come out from his anus. Allah says: ﴿And they are given to drink boiling water, which cuts their intestines﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. And Allah says: ﴿And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal that scorches the faces. What a wretched drink!﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. [Al-Tirmidhi] recorded it and said: it is a gharib (rare) hadith. As for Ubayd Allah ibn Busr, from whom Safwan ibn 'Amr related the hadith of Abu Umama, he may be the brother of 'Abd Allah ibn Busr.

(Gulping it down, yatajarra'uhu): meaning he sips it in sips, not all at once, because of its bitterness and heat.

(And he can hardly swallow it, wa-la yakadu yusighuhu): meaning he cannot swallow it. It is said: *jara'a al-ma'* and *ijtara'ahu* and *tajarra'ahu* have the same meaning. *Sagha al-sharab fi al-halq yasugh sawgh* means when a drink goes down the throat smoothly and easily, and *asaghahu Allah isaghah* means Allah made it go down. The word *yakad* here is a connective (silah), meaning he swallows it only after difficulty. Allah says: ﴿And they hardly did it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71], meaning they did it after delay. Therefore He says: ﴿By which what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted﴾ [al-Hajj: 20], and this indicates swallowing. Ibn 'Abbas said: he allows it to pass down but it does not go through easily.

(And death comes to him from every place): Ibn 'Abbas said: the causes of death come to him from every direction, from his right and left, from above and below, from in front of him and behind him, as in His saying: ﴿For them there will be layers of fire above them and layers beneath them﴾ [al-Zumar: 16]. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: death comes to him from every part of his body, even to the ends of his hair, because of the pains that are in every part of the body. Al-Dahhak said: death truly comes to him from every side and place, even from the big toes of his feet. Al-Akhfash said: it means the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in the Fire, which he called death, and which are among the greatest forms of death. It was also said: no limb of his remains without a kind of punishment assigned to it; if he were to die seventy times, that would be easier for him than one kind of it in a single moment: either a serpent biting him, or a scorpion stinging him (talsibuhu, meaning stings him; tasfa'uhu, meaning blackens his face), or fire scorching him, or a shackle on his feet, or a yoke on his neck, or a chain by which he is bound, or a coffin in which he is placed, or the zaqqum tree, or boiling water, or other punishments. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: when the disbeliever in Hell asks for a drink and sees it, he dies a death; when he draws near it, he dies a death; when he drinks it, he dies a death. This is His statement: ﴿And death comes to him from every place, but he is not dead﴾. Al-Dahhak said: he does not die so that he may rest. Ibn Jurayj said: his soul is caught in his throat, so it does not come out of his mouth and he dies, and it does not return to its place in his body so that life benefits him. A parallel to this is His statement: ﴿Neither dying therein nor living﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74]. It was also said: Allah creates in his body pains, each of which is like the pain of death. It was also said: "but he is not dead" because the severe pangs of death are prolonged upon him and its agonies extend over him, so that this increases his punishment. I say: from this it appears that he dies, but that is not so, according to His statement: ﴿Nothing will be decreed for them so that they die, nor will their punishment be lightened for them﴾ [Fatir: 36], and the Sunnah has come with this. The state of the disbelievers is that of one over whom the agonies of death always prevail. And Allah knows best.

(And behind him): meaning in front of him.

(A severe punishment): meaning intense, with continuous pains without slackening. From this is His statement: ﴿And let them find in you harshness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123], meaning severity and strength. Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, concerning the statement of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And behind him is a severe punishment﴾, said: it is the holding of breath.

*Neither one present who can escape it, nor one who is hidden from it.*

*While my people Tamim and the deserts are behind me?*

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 18–20:

The grammarians differed regarding the case of "مَثَلُ" (mathal, "parable/example"). Sibawayh said: it is in the nominative by virtue of being the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted. The implied sense is: "And among what is recited to you or related to you is the parable of those who disbelieve in their Lord," then he begins anew and says: "their deeds are like ashes" (a'maluhum ka-ramad), meaning "like the likeness of ashes upon which the wind blows violently" (ishtaddat bihi al-rih).

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "The parable of those who disbelieve, in what is recited to you, is that their deeds are like ashes." According to al-Farra', it is by way of cancelling "mathal" (ilghaʾ al-mathal), the sense being: "And those who disbelieve in their Lord, their deeds are like ashes." It is also reported from him that it is by way of omitting a modifier (hadhf mudaf), the sense being: "The parable of the deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord is like ashes." The first of these was mentioned from him by al-Mahdawi, and the second by al-Qushayri and al-Tha'labi.

It is also permissible that it be the subject (mubtada'), as one says: "The description of so-and-so is 'asmar" (dark-complexioned), so "mathal" here carries the meaning of "sifah" (description).

It is also permissible in speech to put "a'maluhum" in the genitive as a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from "alladhina" (those who). This connects with His words: "And every obstinate tyrant has failed" (wa-khaba kullu jabbarin 'anid). The meaning is: "Their deeds are nullified and unaccepted."

Al-ramad (ashes) is what remains after a thing has burned. So God struck this verse as a parable for the deeds of the disbelievers, in that He obliterates them just as a violent wind scatters ashes on a stormy day. Al-'asf (stormy) means the intensity of the wind. That was so because they associated others with God, the Exalted, in it.

Regarding the attribution of "stormy" to the day, there are three opinions. The first: although "al-'usuf" belongs to the wind, the day may be described by it, because the wind occurs in it; so it is permissible to say "a stormy day," just as one says "a hot day" and "a cold day," while cold and heat are in both. The second: that "fi yawmin 'asif" intends the wind, because it was mentioned at the beginning of the phrase, as the poet said:

"When there comes a day, its sun darkened, eclipsed" (idha ja'a yawmun muzlimu al-shams kasif)

He means "eclipsed the sun," but omitted it because its mention had already passed. Al-Harawi mentioned both of these. The third: that it is an attribute of the wind, but since it came after "day," its i'rab was made to follow it, as is said: "the burrow of a dhabb (lizard), ruined" (juhru dabbin kharib). Al-Tha'labi and al-Mawardi mentioned this.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr read "fi yawmin 'asif" with the day put in annexation to "'asif." Whoever reads it this way has placed the attribute in the position of the described noun, meaning "in a day of stormy wind." The reading of Nafi' and Ibn Ja'far is "al-riyah" (the winds), in the plural.

(La yaqdiruna) refers to the disbelievers.

(Mimma kasabu 'ala shay') means, in the Hereafter: from the reward of what they did of righteousness in the world, since it was nullified by their disbelief.

(Dhalika huwa al-dalal al-ba'id) means the great loss. He called it great and far-reaching because its recovery is impossible after death.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that God created the heavens and the earth with truth?﴾ The seeing here is seeing of the heart, because the meaning is: "Has your knowledge not reached Him?" Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "Khaliq al-samawati wal-ard" (Creator of the heavens and the earth). The meaning of "bil-haqq" is that they serve as evidence of His power.

(In yasha' yudhhibkum) O people, meaning: He is able to annihilate just as He was able to bring things into existence, so do not disobey Him, for if you disobey Him (yudhhibkum wa-ya'ti bikhalqin jadid), He will remove you and bring a new creation better and more obedient than you, since if they were like the first ones there would be no benefit in the replacement.

(Wa-ma dhalika 'ala Allahi bi-'aziz) means: not inaccessible or unattainable.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 18–20:

The grammarians differed regarding the case of "مَثَلُ" (mathal, "parable/example"). Sibawayh said: it is in the nominative by virtue of being the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted. The implied sense is: "And among what is recited to you or related to you is the parable of those who disbelieve in their Lord," then he begins anew and says: "their deeds are like ashes" (a'maluhum ka-ramad), meaning "like the likeness of ashes upon which the wind blows violently" (ishtaddat bihi al-rih).

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "The parable of those who disbelieve, in what is recited to you, is that their deeds are like ashes." According to al-Farra', it is by way of cancelling "mathal" (ilghaʾ al-mathal), the sense being: "And those who disbelieve in their Lord, their deeds are like ashes." It is also reported from him that it is by way of omitting a modifier (hadhf mudaf), the sense being: "The parable of the deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord is like ashes." The first of these was mentioned from him by al-Mahdawi, and the second by al-Qushayri and al-Tha'labi.

It is also permissible that it be the subject (mubtada'), as one says: "The description of so-and-so is 'asmar" (dark-complexioned), so "mathal" here carries the meaning of "sifah" (description).

It is also permissible in speech to put "a'maluhum" in the genitive as a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from "alladhina" (those who). This connects with His words: "And every obstinate tyrant has failed" (wa-khaba kullu jabbarin 'anid). The meaning is: "Their deeds are nullified and unaccepted."

Al-ramad (ashes) is what remains after a thing has burned. So God struck this verse as a parable for the deeds of the disbelievers, in that He obliterates them just as a violent wind scatters ashes on a stormy day. Al-'asf (stormy) means the intensity of the wind. That was so because they associated others with God, the Exalted, in it.

Regarding the attribution of "stormy" to the day, there are three opinions. The first: although "al-'usuf" belongs to the wind, the day may be described by it, because the wind occurs in it; so it is permissible to say "a stormy day," just as one says "a hot day" and "a cold day," while cold and heat are in both. The second: that "fi yawmin 'asif" intends the wind, because it was mentioned at the beginning of the phrase, as the poet said:

"When there comes a day, its sun darkened, eclipsed" (idha ja'a yawmun muzlimu al-shams kasif)

He means "eclipsed the sun," but omitted it because its mention had already passed. Al-Harawi mentioned both of these. The third: that it is an attribute of the wind, but since it came after "day," its i'rab was made to follow it, as is said: "the burrow of a dhabb (lizard), ruined" (juhru dabbin kharib). Al-Tha'labi and al-Mawardi mentioned this.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr read "fi yawmin 'asif" with the day put in annexation to "'asif." Whoever reads it this way has placed the attribute in the position of the described noun, meaning "in a day of stormy wind." The reading of Nafi' and Ibn Ja'far is "al-riyah" (the winds), in the plural.

(La yaqdiruna) refers to the disbelievers.

(Mimma kasabu 'ala shay') means, in the Hereafter: from the reward of what they did of righteousness in the world, since it was nullified by their disbelief.

(Dhalika huwa al-dalal al-ba'id) means the great loss. He called it great and far-reaching because its recovery is impossible after death.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that God created the heavens and the earth with truth?﴾ The seeing here is seeing of the heart, because the meaning is: "Has your knowledge not reached Him?" Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "Khaliq al-samawati wal-ard" (Creator of the heavens and the earth). The meaning of "bil-haqq" is that they serve as evidence of His power.

(In yasha' yudhhibkum) O people, meaning: He is able to annihilate just as He was able to bring things into existence, so do not disobey Him, for if you disobey Him (yudhhibkum wa-ya'ti bikhalqin jadid), He will remove you and bring a new creation better and more obedient than you, since if they were like the first ones there would be no benefit in the replacement.

(Wa-ma dhalika 'ala Allahi bi-'aziz) means: not inaccessible or unattainable.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 14, verse 21–22:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will come forth before Allah, all of them﴾. That is, they will come forth from their graves, meaning on the Day of Resurrection. Al-buruz (emergence) is manifestation, and al-biraz is a wide open place because of its visibility. From this comes the expression imra'ah barzah, meaning a woman who appears [[Al-Misbah says: "Imra'ah barzah" is a chaste woman who goes out to men and converses with them, and it refers to a woman who has aged and passed the limit of those who are veiled. Imra'ah barzah also means a woman whose attractions are visible. Al-Raghib said: this is because of the elevation of her chastity, not because the word necessarily implies that.]] before the people. So the meaning of "they came forth" (baraza) is that they appeared from their graves. The verb is in the past form while its meaning is future, and this is linked to His saying: ﴿and every obstinate tyrant will be disappointed﴾. That is, they will draw near when they seek victory and are destroyed, then they will be raised for the reckoning and they will come forth before Allah, all of them, with nothing to conceal them from Him by any concealer. "Li-Llah" means on account of the command of Allah to them to come forth.

(﴿Then the weak will say﴾) meaning the followers, (﴿to those who were arrogant﴾) and they are the leaders.

(﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾). It is permissible for taba' to be a verbal noun, with the implied sense "possessors of following." It is also permissible for it to be tabi', like hāris and haras, khādim and khadam, rāsid and rasad, and bāqir and baqar [[Baqar: he split and widened.]].

(﴿So will you avail us against the punishment of Allah in anything?﴾) That is, will you ward off from us a portion of it? "Min" is extra. It is said aghnā 'anhu when one wards off harm from him, and aghnāhu when one brings benefit to him.

(﴿They will say: "If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you."﴾) That is, if Allah had guided us to faith, we would have guided you to it. It has also been said: if Allah had guided us to the path of Paradise, we would have guided you to it. And it has been said: if Allah had saved us from the punishment, we would have saved you from it.

(﴿It is all the same for us﴾) This is an inchoative clause whose predicate is "whether we rage or we endure". That is: (﴿It is all the same for us whether we rage or we endure; there is for us no place of escape﴾), that is, no refuge or shelter. It is permissible for maḥīṣ to be a verbal noun and also a noun of place. It is said: fulān ḥāṣa 'an kadhā, meaning he fled and turned aside, yaḥīṣu ḥays, ḥuyūṣ, and ḥayaṣān. The meaning is: we have no way by which we can keep far from the Fire.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The people of the Fire, when the punishment intensifies upon them, will say: 'Come, let us endure.' So they endure for five hundred years. Then when they see that this does not benefit them, they say: 'Come, let us rage.' So they rage and cry out for five hundred years. Then when they see that this does not benefit them, they say: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we rage or we endure; there is for us no place of escape﴾."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: It has been mentioned that the people of the Fire say to one another: "O people! Trouble and punishment have descended upon you, as you see. Come, let us endure, for perhaps endurance will benefit us just as the people of obedience endured in obedience to Allah, and endurance benefited them when they endured." So they agreed upon endurance and endured. Their endurance lengthened, so they raged, and they called out: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we rage or we endure; there is for us no place of escape﴾, that is, no deliverance. At that point Iblis stood and said: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you a promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. And I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieved in your associating me [with Allah] before﴾. He means: I am not one who can avail you anything. This is a long hadith, and we have written it in full in the book "al-Tadhkirah".

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided﴾. Al-Hasan said: Iblis will stand on the Day of Resurrection as a preacher in Hell, upon a pulpit of fire, and all of creation will hear him. The meaning of "when the matter has been decided" is that the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, as will be explained in Surah Maryam [[See vol. 11, p. 105.]], upon her be peace.

(﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth﴾) meaning the resurrection, Paradise, the Fire, the reward of the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient. So He fulfilled His promise to you. And I promised you that there would be no resurrection, no Paradise, no Fire, no reward, and no punishment, so I failed you. Ibn al-Mubarak related from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in the hadith of intercession, that he said: "Jesus will say: 'I will direct you to the unlettered Prophet.' So they will come to me, and Allah will permit me to rise. My seat will be perfumed with the finest scent anyone has ever smelled, until I come to my Lord, and He will grant me intercession and make for me a light from the hair of my head to the nail of my foot. Then the disbelievers will say: 'The believers have found someone to intercede for them; who will intercede for us?' They will say: 'None but Iblis, for he is the one who misled us.' So they will come to him and say: 'The believers have found someone to intercede for them, so intercede for us, for you misled us.' His seat will then be overturned by the foulest smell anyone has ever smelled. Then their wailing will grow intense, and at that point he will say: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you but I failed you﴾..." (the verse).

"Wa'd al-haqq" (the promise of truth) is the attribution of a thing to its qualifier, as in the expression masjid al-jami' (the congregational mosque). Al-Farra' said: the Basrans said: "He promised you the promise of the true day," or "He promised you the promise of the true promise, so He fulfilled it for you," and the verbal noun was omitted because the situation indicates it.

(﴿And I had no authority over you﴾) that is, no proof or evidence. That is, I did not show you any proof for what I promised you and what I adorned for you in the world. (﴿except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾) that is, I led you astray, and you followed me. It has also been said: I did not compel you to what I called you to. "Illa an da'awtukum" is an exceptive clause that is disconnected (munqati'), meaning: rather, I called you by whispering, and you responded to me by your own choice. (﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾.) It has also been said: "And I had no authority over you" means over your hearts and the place of your faith, but I called you and you responded to me. This is on the view that he addressed the disobedient believer and the denying disbeliever. But this is open to question, because of His saying: "when the matter has been decided," which indicates that he addressed the disbelievers rather than the disobedient monotheists. And Allah knows best.

(﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾) when you come to me without any proof.

(﴿I cannot help you﴾) that is, I cannot rescue you.

(﴿Nor can you help me﴾) that is, you cannot rescue me. Al-sarikh and al-mustasrikh is one who seeks help and assistance, while al-musrikh is one who rescues. Salamah ibn Jandal said:

We, when a terrified crier came to us, and his cry was the striking of the shin-bones [[Al-zanabib (plural of zanbub) is the dry bone of the shin. Qar' al-zanbub means that a man strikes the shin of a camel to make it kneel so he can mount it, and the intended meaning here is swiftness of response.]]

And Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"Do not rage; indeed I am not one who can help you, and there is no aid or victory from me for you."

It is said: sarakha fulan, meaning he sought aid; he cries out, sarkhan, surakhan, and sarkhah. Istarkha is the same in meaning as sarakha. Al-tasarrukh is the effort to cry out. Al-musrikh is the rescuer, and al-mustasrikh is the one who seeks rescue; from it one says: istasrakhani fa-asrakhtuhu. Al-sarikh is the sound of the one seeking rescue. Al-sarikh also means the crier, who is both the rescuer and the one seeking rescue, and it is among the words with opposite meanings, as al-Jawhari said. The reading of the common people is "bi-musrikhiyya" with a fatha on the ya'. Al-A'mash and Hamzah read "bi-musrikhiyyi" with a kasra on the ya'. Originally it is bi-musrakhiyyina, so the nun was dropped for the idafah, and the ya' of the plural was assimilated into the ya' of the idafah. Whoever uses fatha does so because of the doubling, and because when the letter before the ya' of the idafah is sukun, fatha is required there, like hawaya and 'asaya. If the letter before it is vowelled, both fatha and sukun are permitted, like ghulami and ghulamati. Whoever uses kasra does so because two sakins meet, so it is moved to kasra, since the ya' is a sister of the kasra. Al-Farra' said: Hamzah's reading is an error on his part, and few of them are free from error [[i.e., of al-Farra']]. Al-Zajjaj said: this is a poor reading, and it has no justification except a weak one. Qutrub said: this is the dialect of the Banu Yarbu', who add a ya' to the ya' of the idafah. Al-Qushayri said: what settles this is that whatever is established by mass-transmission (tawatur) from the Prophet ﷺ cannot be described as an error, ugly, or poor. Rather, it is eloquent in the Qur'an, and there is something more eloquent than it. Perhaps these people meant that other than what Hamzah recited is more eloquent.

(﴿Indeed, I disbelieved in your associating me [with Allah] before﴾) that is, I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah, Exalted is He, in obedience. So "lamma" here carries the sense of a verbal noun. Ibn Juraij said: "Indeed, I disbelieve today in what you used to claim in the world of associating others with Allah, Exalted is He." Qatadah said: "Indeed, I disobeyed Allah." Al-Thawri said: "I disbelieve in your obedience to me in the world."

(﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment﴾). In these verses there is a refutation of the Qadariyya, the Mu'tazila, the Imamiyya, and whoever follows their path. Look at the saying of the leaders: ﴿If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you﴾, and the saying of Iblis: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you a promise of truth﴾, how they acknowledged the truth concerning the attributes of Allah, Exalted is He, while they were in the depths of the Fire. As He says in another place: ﴿Every time a group is cast into it, its keepers will ask them...﴾ [al-Mulk: 8] up to His saying: ﴿So they will acknowledge their sin﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 212.]] [al-Mulk: 11]. Their acknowledgment of the truth in the depths of Laza is of no benefit. Acknowledgment benefits its owner only in the world. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins; they mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil; perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness﴾ [[See vol. 8, pp. 241 and 313.]] [al-Tawbah: 102]. And "perhaps" from Allah is binding [[That is, what it indicates is certain to occur from Allah.]].

**Issue two concerns the verse: "Have you not seen how Allah has struck a parable"**

When Allah the Exalted mentioned the parable of the deeds of the disbelievers, that they are like ashes which the wind blows violently on a stormy day, He then mentioned the parable of the words of the believers and other things. Then He explained that parable by saying: (a good word) is the tree, so He omitted it because the context indicates it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The good word is 'there is no god but Allah,' and the good tree is the believer." Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: "The good word is faith (iman)." 'Ata' al-'Awfi and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "It is the believer himself." Mujahid also said, together with 'Ikrimah: "The tree is the palm tree." It is possible that the meaning is: the root of the word in the heart of the believer, which is faith, is likened to the palm tree in its place of growth, and the elevation of his deed into the sky is likened to the elevation of the palm's branches, and Allah's reward for him is likened to the fruit.

It has been related from the hadith of Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The likeness of faith is like a firm tree: faith is its roots, prayer is its trunk, zakat is its branches, fasting is its boughs, the ta'adhdhi (…) for Allah is its growth, good character is its leaves, and abstaining from what Allah has forbidden is its fruit." It is also possible that the meaning is: the root of the palm tree is firm in the earth, that is, its roots drink from the earth, and the sky waters it from above, so it is thriving and growing.

Al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: A qina' (a tray made of palm fronds, in which food and fruit are placed) containing fresh dates was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "The likeness of a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firm and whose branches are in the sky, giving its fruit every season by the permission of its Lord" – he said – "It is the palm tree. And the likeness of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability." – he said – "It is the colocynth (handhal)." It has also been related from Anas that this was his statement [and he said]: and it is more sound (ṣaḥīḥ). (That is, al-Tirmidhi said: the halted (mawquf) hadith is more sound.)

Al-Daraqutni related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "Allah has struck a parable: a good word like a good tree, whose root is firm," then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what it is?" It occurred to my mind that it was the palm tree. Al-Suhayli said: What has been related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, that it is the coconut tree (jawzat al-Hind), is not sound, because it is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "Among the trees there is a tree whose leaf does not fall, and it is the likeness of the believer. Tell me what it is" – then he said – "It is the palm tree." Malik related it in al-Muwatta' from the narration of Ibn al-Qasim and others, except Yahya, who omitted it from his narration. The compilers of the authentic collections also related it, and al-Harith ibn Usama added to it an addition worth a journey (i.e., one must travel to narrate it), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "It is the palm tree, of which not a single fingertip falls off, and likewise the believer, whose supplication does not fall off."

So this explains the meaning of the hadith and the comparison. Al-Ghaznawi also mentioned from him (peace be upon him): "The likeness of the believer is like the palm tree: if you keep company with him, he benefits you; if you sit with him, he benefits you; if you consult him, he benefits you. Like the palm tree, every part of it is useful." And he said: "Eat from your aunt" – meaning the palm tree. It was created from the surplus of the clay of Adam (peace be upon him). Likewise, its head remains and its heart lives, and its fruit comes from the mixing of male and female. It has been said: since it is the tree most similar to a human being, it was likened to him, because every tree, when its top is cut, its branches spread from its sides, but the palm, when its top is cut, dries up and perishes entirely. Also, it resembles humans and the rest of the animals in pollination, because it does not bear fruit until it is pollinated. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best property is a row of palms that have been pollinated and a mare that is fertile" (the sikkah is a row of palms set in line; the ma'mūrah is one abundant in offspring and produce; he meant the best property is that which produces offspring or crops). Al-ibar means pollination, and its explanation will come in Surat al-Hijr (See vol. 10, p. 15). Also, it is because it is from the surplus of Adam's clay. It is said that when Allah the Mighty and Majestic formed Adam from clay, a piece of clay remained, so He shaped it with His hand and planted it in the Garden of Eden. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Honour your aunt." They said: "And who is our aunt, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The palm tree."

**(It gives its fruit every season)** Al-Rabi' said: "Every season" means morning and evening; likewise the deed of the believer ascends at the beginning and end of the day. Ibn 'Abbas also said this. And it was related from him: "It gives its fruit every season," he said: it is a tree of al-Hind (jawzat al-Hind, the coconut tree) that is never without fruit; it bears in every month. The deed of the believer for Allah the Mighty and Majestic at every time is likened to the palm tree that gives its fruit at different times. Al-Dahhak said: every hour of night or day, in winter and summer, it yields at all times; likewise the believer is never without good at all times. Al-Nahhas said: These sayings are close in meaning and not contradictory, because the word hin (ḥīn) according to all the lexicographers, except for those who deviated among them, means "a time," which applies to a short or long period. Al-Asma'i recited the verse of al-Nabigha:

"The charmers warned one another of its evil venom… it releases him at times, and at times it returns to him."
[The verse describes his snake: "the charmers warned one another" means they warned each other not to approach it. "It releases him at times, and at times it returns" means it hides the pain from the healthy one at times, and at other times it presses hard on him. Another version reads: "from the evil of its hearing," meaning it does not respond to the charmer, not that it is deaf, as they say: "more attentive than a snake."]

This shows you that hin means a time. So faith is firmly established in the heart of the believer, and his deed, his speech and his glorification rise high in the sky like the elevation of the palm's branches, and what he gains of the blessing and reward of faith is like what is obtained from the palm's fruit throughout all seasons of the year: from the rutab (fresh dates), the busr (unripe dates), the balah, the zahw (dates that have turned colour), the tamr (dried dates), and the ṭal' (the spathe/flower cluster). In a report from Ibn 'Abbas: the tree is a tree in Paradise that bears fruit at every time.

**(a parable)**: "mathalan" is the object of "ḍaraba," and "kalimatan" is in apposition to it. The kāf in His saying "like a tree" (kashajarah) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "kalimatan," the sense being: a good word compared to a good tree.

**The second issue** concerns the saying of Allah the Exalted: **"It gives its fruit every season."** Since trees give their fruit once a year, this indicates the ruling on the word ḥīn. For this reason we say: whoever swears that he will not speak to so-and-so for a ḥīn, or that he will not do such-and-such for a ḥīn, the ḥīn is a year. The word ḥīn occurs in another place with a meaning referring to a longer period, as in His saying: **"Has there come upon man a period of time from eternity?"** (al-Insan: 1). It was said in the tafsir: forty years. 'Ikrimah related that a man said: "If I do such-and-such until a ḥīn, then my slave is free." He came to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and asked him. He asked me about it, and I said: "Among the ḥīn is a ḥīn that cannot be determined." (His saying): **"And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time"** (al-Anbiya': 111). I think you should withhold what is between the cutting of the palm (ṣirām) and its bearing of fruit. It seemed to please him. This is also the view of Abu Hanifa regarding ḥīn: that it is six months, following 'Ikrimah and others. What the scholars said about ḥīn has already been covered fully in al-Baqarah (See vol. 1, p. 321 onwards), and praise be to Allah.

"And they are like dodder, with neither root nor leaf,
Nor breeze, nor shade, nor date."
[Its completion: "and no shade, and no dates." He means that they have no lineage and no ancestry. The reading in al-Lisan and al-Taj is: "it is the dodder."]

"It is the expulsion that uproots your root,
